scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y sus herederos
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: La línea de art rock que reivindica el postpunk no es la del progresivo sinfónico sino la que va de The Velvet Underground al krautrock y al glam intelectual, fiel al principio minimalista «menos es más». Durante el «páramo» de los setenta, un racimo de espíritus afines unidos por su deuda con la Velvet (Lou Reed, John Cale, Nico, Iggy Pop, Bowie, Eno) colaboró en distintas combinaciones y sostuvo a los hipsters.

scenes.name: Detroit: MC5 y Stooges
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La ciudad más industrial de EE UU y cuartel de los elementos más extremistas de la contracultura: un rock'n'roll feroz y ruidoso se convierte en la voz de los obreros y de sus hijos. Los MC5 de John Sinclair, ala revolucionaria de las revueltas estudiantiles (Kick Out The Jams, «el equivalente rockero de una explosión nuclear»); los Stooges de Iggy Pop, síntesis de Chuck Berry, Rolling Stones, Velvet Underground y Doors que inventa el punk-rock («1970») y el voodoobilly («TV Eye»). Un nuevo rock'n'roll fundado en la violencia extrema.

podcast.title: Band Formation (Late 1967)
podcast.body: The Stooges were formed by James Osterberg (later Iggy Pop) and a group of "local degenerates" one night in Detroit, inspired by a bag of dope and a Three Stooges movie marathon on television. "One night, over a bag of dope and a three-stooge's movie marathon on television, he and a bunch of local degenerates decided to form a band that they called the Stooge's."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Debut Performance (October 31, 1967)
podcast.body: The band, initially called Iggy and the Psychedelic Stooges, made their debut on October 31, 1967, in Ann Arbor, Michigan. They were characterized by a loud, spontaneous, sloppy, fuzzy, arrogant, violent, angry, and powerful sound. "And on October 31, 1967, Iggy and the psychedelic studios made their debut in Ann Arbor, Michigan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: First Gig (Halloween 1967)
podcast.body: The Stooges' debut performance was on Halloween 1967 at their headquarters on State Street in Ann Arbor, described as "weird." Iggy wore an aluminum foil wig and played a Hawaiian guitar tuned only to E, Scott played oil drums with ball-peen hammers, and Dave created reverb effects by banging on Ron's amplifier. Despite the unconventional and "awful" performance, both band and audience, being high, considered it a success. "Iggy wore a wig made of strands of aluminum foil and played a Hawaiian guitar with every string tune to E."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: First Show Guitar Malfunction (October 31, 1967)
podcast.body: On the day of their inaugural performance, Iggy Pop's Hawaiian guitar was rendered useless because guitarist Ron Ashton had painted it, pickups included. Iggy's subsequent abandonment of the guitar and spontaneous, wild dancing, combined with his pants falling down, led to the birth of his legendary, audience-loved punk rock stage antics. "So when the Stooge's hit the stage, Iggy's guitar was completely useless because of the paint."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Formation and Members (1967)
podcast.body: The band was formed in 1967 by James Newell Osterberg (Iggy), brothers Ron and Scott Ashton, and Dave Alexander. Iggy, who was a known drummer in Ann Arbor, befriended Ron Ashton, leading to Scott joining, and then Dave Alexander, a high school dropout who had traveled the UK in search of the meaning of The Beatles. "These four guys decided to form a band with Iggy out front and on keyboards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Jim Morrison's Influence (1967)
podcast.body: On October 20, 1967, Iggy attended a Doors show at the University of Michigan and was greatly inspired by Jim Morrison's drunken behavior and provocative interactions with the audience, which influenced Iggy's own stage persona. "Iggy was there and he was inspired by Jim Morrison's drunkenness in the way he provoked the audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Early Professional Gigs and "Osterizer" (1968)
podcast.body: The band's first professional gig was opening for the Amboy Dukes (featuring Ted Nugent) on January 20, 1968, followed by an opening slot for Blood Sweat and Tears on March 3, 1968. During these shows, Iggy notably played a homemade instrument called the "Osterizer," which was a vacuum cleaner attached to a blender, although he soon abandoned it due to amplification difficulties. "And was the singer playing a vacuum cleaner? Yes, yes it was. And was it attached to a blender? And yeah, it was."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: First Proper Public Performance (March 1968)
podcast.body: The band's first official public performance took place in March 1968. The opening act for this show was unusual: a food processor (blender with water) roaring through the PA system for about 15 minutes. "The first proper public performance came in March of 1968. The opening act for this show was a food processor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Early Stage Diving (1969)
podcast.body: Iggy Pop is noted for performing stage diving with The Stooges as early as 1969. This makes him one of the earliest documented figures engaging in this behavior, which later became common at punk and rock shows. "Iggy Pop was doing this with the Stooges as far back as 1969."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Moshing

podcast.title: Drug Addiction and Lineup Changes (Late 1970)
podcast.body: By late 1970, Iggy and Scott Ashton were severely addicted to heroin. Bass player Dave Alexander was fired for being too drunk to perform at a gig. New bass players cycled through, and a second guitarist, James Williamson, was added, but the band struggled with stability. "By the end of 1970, Iggy and Scott Ashton were serious hairwind junkies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Extreme Stage Antics (1970)
podcast.body: By the spring of 1970, The Stooges' live performances became even more extreme and out of control. Iggy would often get naked, cut himself with broken glass, and smear himself with substances like raw meat and peanut butter. Audiences attended primarily for the spectacle, rather than the music. "Iggy was just out of control, often getting naked, cutting himself with broken glass, and smearing things like raw meat and peanut butter all over himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Meeting David Bowie (September 7, 1971)
podcast.body: While in New York "sponging off a friend," Iggy Pop met David Bowie on September 7, 1971. Bowie, who was on the verge of launching his Ziggy Stardust phase, was influenced by Iggy, choosing the name Ziggy partly due to Iggy's persona. "The date was September 7th of 1971. Bowie was about to launch into his Ziggy stardust phase. That character was to be in part inspired by Iggy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Elton John's Attempted Signing and Gorilla Prank (1973)
podcast.body: Elton John, in a competitive rivalry with David Bowie, attempted to show support for and potentially sign The Stooges to his new record label. This led to a surprise visit where Elton, in a gorilla suit, crashed their stage in October 1973, startling Iggy Pop who was heavily under the influence of Quaaludes. "Elton thought he'd have a little fun with Bowie and his relationship with the Stooges, and in the process, maybe he could sign them to his new record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stupid History: The Music Version 1

podcast.title: Band Breakup (1974)
podcast.body: The band broke up in 1974. This event directly contributed to Iggy Pop's subsequent decline into a severe state of drug addiction and homelessness. "In 1974, his band, the stooge's head, broken up and Iggy was reduced to a babbling, wandering junkie prone to blockouts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People

podcast.title: Confrontation with Biker Gang (Early 1974)
podcast.body: By early 1974, the band's behavior was completely out of control. During a gig in Wayne, Michigan, a biker gang called the Scorpions heckled Iggy Pop for his skimpy, skin-tight leopard costume. Iggy confronted them, resulting in eggs and bottles being thrown at the stage. "By early 1974, things had really gotten out of control."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Iggy's Arrest and Hospitalization (October 1974)
podcast.body: In October 1974, Iggy Pop was arrested for being "aggressively strung out" at an LA burger joint. He was subsequently admitted to the UCLA Neuropsychiatric Hospital, where he detoxed and underwent psychiatric evaluation in an 8x4 room for several weeks. "Iggy was arrested for being aggressively strung out in an LA burger joint. He ended up at the UCLA Neurosyche Atric Hospital."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Last Original Show (February 9, 1974)
podcast.body: The final show played by The Stooges before their first long hiatus was on February 9, 1974, at The Rock'n'Roll Farm, a biker bar in Wayne, Michigan. Iggy, wearing a pink leotard, provoked the biker audience with insults during a 45-minute rendition of "Louis Louis," leading to eggs and bottles being thrown. Iggy then confronted a large biker, was punched in the face, and the band left the stage, effectively ending their run. "The last show the studios played together was at a club called The Rock'n'Roll Farm in Wayne, Michigan."

podcast.title: Violent Breakup (1974)
podcast.body: The Stooges ultimately "exploded" on February 9, 1974, amidst a chaotic "haze of heroin, insanity, and debt." "The Stooges finally exploded on February 9th 1974 in a haze of heroin, insanity, and debt."

podcast.body: Ron Ashton died of a heart attack at the age of 60, approximately two years after the release of the reunion album *The Weirdness*. The band subsequently continued with James Williamson returning on guitar. "And then Ron Ashton died of a heart attack. He made it to 60 years old."

podcast.title: Acknowledged by Sex Pistols
podcast.body: Fans, including members of the Sex Pistols, later acknowledged that Iggy Pop was indeed the "Godfather of Punk," recognizing The Stooges' foundational role in the genre. "Fans like the Sex Festels would later acknowledge that Iggy was, yes, the godfather of punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Ann Arbor Formation
podcast.body: The Stooges formed in Ann Arbor, Michigan, in 1967, featuring a young Iggy Pop as their frontman. Their primary goal was not to achieve a sophisticated or virtuous sound but rather to be noisy and animalistic, an objective they successfully achieved. "Formado en Anarbor, Michigan en 1967, con un joven y hipópal frente, Destuji no creían sonar sofisticados y virtuosos, creían sonar ruidosos y animales, y lograron."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Appearance on Iggy Pop's "Skull Ring" (Pre-Reunion)
podcast.body: At the suggestion of Iggy Pop's record company, Ron and Scott Ashton appeared on four songs of Iggy's solo album "Skull Ring." While not a full Stooges reunion, this collaboration served as a significant step towards their eventual reformation. "Ron and Scott appeared on four songs in a record that was eventually released under the title Skull Ring. That wasn't an actual Stooges reunion. These guys were just hired to play on Iggy's record, but it was close."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Band Breakup and Legendary Status
podcast.body: The proposed rematch with the Scorpions never happened, as The Stooges broke up shortly after the incident. This true story cemented their legend as "America's most dangerous rock and roll band." "That never happened, blessedly, because the Stooges then broke up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Band Disintegration
podcast.body: The Stooges "finally blew apart," leading to Iggy Pop's severe mental health crisis and eventual hospitalization, described as a "babbling, strung out freak prone to blockouts and random acts of violence." "When the Stooages finally blew apart, Iggy had nowhere to go but a psychiatric hospital in Los Angeles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Band Name Origin ("Psychedelic Stooges")
podcast.body: The name originated during a drug-fueled session at the Ashton house in 1967 where the band members were watching "The Three Stooges" on TV while high on acid. Initially, they suggested "The Psychedelic Stooges" but it was later shortened to just "The Stooges" as no one could remember how to spell "psychedelic." "When they were very, very high, they were watching the three stuages on TV and somebody suggested I know we'll just call ourselves the psychedelic stuages."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Blueprint for Punk
podcast.body: The Stooges' three studio albums and the famous live bootleg "Metallic KO" served as crucial blueprints for the punk music that emerged in the 1970s and 80s. Their nihilistic and violent style profoundly influenced future bands. "Those three studio albums and that famous bootleg became blueprints for the punk that was to follow in the 1970s and 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Bowie's Intervention and *Raw Power* Production
podcast.body: David Bowie, then on a hot streak with significant industry power, bonded with Iggy Pop. He convinced Iggy, Ron and Scott Ashton, and James Williamson to move to England to record *Raw Power* for Columbia Records, effectively resurrecting the band. "Bowie was on a hot streak and thus he had power. And after bonding with Iggy, he convinced him, the Ashton brothers in James Williamson, to come to England where they'd all make a record for Columbia Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Bowie's Support During Hospitalization
podcast.body: During Iggy Pop's hospitalization in 1974, he had only two visitors: David Bowie and Bowie's costume designer, Ola Hudson (mother of Saul Hudson, later known as Slash). Bowie, despite his own struggles with drugs, played a crucial role as Iggy's and ultimately The Stooges' savior. "He had two visitors. One was David Bowie and the other was Bowie's costume designer, a woman named Ola Hudson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Collapse and Iggy's Hospitalization
podcast.body: Following their struggles, The Stooges couldn't maintain cohesion, leading to their eventual collapse. This period saw Iggy Pop's personal struggles escalate, resulting in him ending up in a mental hospital. David Bowie, a devoted admirer and patron, was Iggy's sole visitor during this time. "Of course, the Stooges couldn't hold it together and everything collapsed. Iggy eventually ended up at a mental hospital, where his only visitor was, you guessed it, David Bowie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

podcast.title: Commercial Failure and Punk Legacy
podcast.body: The Stooges' albums, though critically acclaimed in retrospect, were largely commercial failures during their initial release due to their raw and primitive sound, which was ahead of its time. Despite this, their debut album is considered one of the most important pre-punk records, contributing to Iggy's legend as the "godfather of punk." "It has gone down on history as being one of the most important pre-punk records of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Confrontational Stage Presence & Stage Diving
podcast.body: The Stooges developed a divisive live reputation, attracting audiences who either loved or hated them. Iggy Pop's performances were characterized by self-destructive, confrontational, and contortionist antics, often involving him being half-naked, and frequently diving into the audience without concern for his or their safety. He is considered a possible inventor of stage diving. "It's quite possible that Iggy was the inventor of stage diving."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Contrast to MC5
podcast.body: While MC5 represented organized rage, The Stooges epitomized the opposite: an empty, primitive scream devoid of ideology, a precursor to the "No Future" sentiment later championed by the Sex Pistols. This stark contrast highlighted the diverse expressions of early punk energy in Detroit. "Si MC5 representaba la rabia organizada, Destuji será lo contrario, un especie de grito vacío, primitivo y sin ideología."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Covered by The Sisters of Mercy
podcast.body: The Stooges were among the artists whose songs were covered by The Sisters of Mercy in their early days, indicating an influence or appreciation within the nascent goth scene. "But in the early days, the Sisters were known for their covers, stooges, bob Dylan, not chocolate if I'm a band, velvet underground, and a killer version of Louis Louis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 5: Goth

podcast.title: Discovery and Signing by Danny Fields
podcast.body: The Stooges came to the attention of Danny Fields, a talent scout for Elektra Records known for signing hippie bands like The Doors. Fields discovered them while in Detroit to check out MC5, and despite his bosses being "stupified" by The Stooges, he convinced Elektra to sign them. "However, the stuages eventually came to the attention of Danny Fields, a talent scout for electro-records who was hired for his ability to find the right hippie bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Dropped by Elektra and Financial Ruin
podcast.body: Due to their escalating drug problems, chaotic gigs (where Iggy was sometimes too stoned to stand), Elektra Records dropped The Stooges. The label also demanded an $11,000 refund on an advance given to the band. The Stooges then entered a nine-month period of inactivity, save for drug use, with Ron Ashton becoming estranged from the group, calling it a "death trip." "So Electra dropped them. Actually, they more than dropped them. They demanded a refund of $11,000 on an advance they had given the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Dropped by Label and Drug Use
podcast.body: Around 1971, The Stooges were dropped from their record label and were deeply entrenched in hard drug use. This period coincided with Jonathan Richmond recording "Roadrunner," highlighting a stark contrast in musical approaches and lifestyles within the alternative scene. "Well, at about the same time Jonathan Richmond was recording Roadrunner, the Stooges were being dropped from their record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

podcast.title: Drug Problems and Chaotic Incidents
podcast.body: The band faced severe drug issues, with Iggy Pop spending time in a mental ward. Other chaotic incidents included a member attempting to drive their 15-foot high truck under a 13-foot high bridge and problems with violent Detroit biker gangs. "Drugs were a big part of their problem. Iggy actually ended up in a mental ward for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Early Influences & Recognition
podcast.body: The Stooges are frequently cited as a major influence by contemporary bands like The White Stripes and The Hives, and by 90s bands such as Jane's Addiction and Nirvana. They also shaped the sound of 80s bands like Sonic Youth and inspired 70s artists like the Sex Pistols, Ramones, and David Bowie to make music. "So the stooges seem to be on everybody's list even though they hardly sold any records in their day and were so messed up that their singer ended up in an asylum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Extreme Behavior and Drug Use
podcast.body: The Stooges were known for their wild and intense performances, with Iggy Pop being particularly unhinged. The band extensively used drugs, including heroin and Angel Dust, leading to self-destructive behavior and an out-of-control reputation. "They were on every drug known to man all the way up to heroin and Angel Dust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Extreme Contrast to Mainstream and Hippie Bands
podcast.body: The Stooges, particularly through Iggy Pop's antics, presented a "crazy" and extreme alternative that starkly contrasted with mainstream acts like The Beatles and The Rolling Stones, and was also distinct from the prevailing hippie groups. "This wasn't anything mainstream bands like the beetles or the stones we're doing. And the hippie groups, certainly weren't into this kind of thing either."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Extreme Performances
podcast.body: The Stooges, featuring Iggy Pop, were known for their "extreme things" performed in America, contributing to the outrageous aesthetic that inspired David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona. "who was doing all kinds of extreme things in America with his band, The Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Financial Troubles and Truck Incident
podcast.body: The Stooges were plagued by debts, including an IRS investigation for unpaid taxes, and bills resulting from an incident where Scott Ashton attempted to drive the band's 14-foot truck under a 13-foot bridge. "They were under investigation by the IRS for non-payment of taxes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: First Breakup and Iggy's Hiatus
podcast.body: Eventually, the band dissolved. Iggy Pop spent the next six months in Florida cutting lawns for retirees. "Eventually, the stuages were done. Iggy spent the next six months in Florida cutting lawns for retirees."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: First Show (Halloween, Year Not Specified)
podcast.body: Iggy Pop formed The Psychedelic Stooges in the summer of 1967, and their first show was a private party held on Halloween. The performance was reportedly so poor that their manager quit and returned to his job as a school teacher. "they played their first show at a private party that Halloween. It wasn't very good, so bad that their manager quit and went back to his job as a school teacher."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Formation and Influence – Post-Drumming for Iggy Pop
podcast.body: After his initial drumming experiences, Iggy Pop moved on from behind the drum kit to start writing songs and formed The Stooges. This band, along with Iggy's subsequent involvement with David Bowie and other experiences, contributed significantly to laying the foundations for modern punk rock. "He started writing songs moved on to the stooges got involved with David Bowie took a lot of LSD and pretty much laid the foundations for modern punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Drummers

podcast.title: Iggy Pop's Beating and Challenge
podcast.body: While the rest of the band fled, Iggy Pop remained to confront the bikers, jumping into the crowd and receiving a severe beating before being dragged out, possibly saving his life. Days later, Iggy appeared on the radio, promoting an upcoming show and boldly challenging the Scorpions to a rematch. "He stayed there to confront the bikers, jumping into the crowd. And he got a pretty good beating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Iggy Pop's Name Origin
podcast.body: James Newell Osterberg adopted the stage name "Iggy" from his previous band, The Iguanas. The "Pop" part was added after he shaved off his eyebrows in a "weird stoned gesture," leading the other band members to comment that he resembled a local drug user named Jim Pop. "The pop part came after Iggy shaved off his eyebrows in some weird stone to gesture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Iggy Pop's Stage Antics
podcast.body: Iggy Pop was notorious for scaring audiences with his antics, which included smearing peanut butter on himself and carving his body with broken glass from bottles thrown at him on stage. "He'd smear peanut butter all over himself and often carve himself up with broken glass from the beer bottles that were thrown at him on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Iggy Pop's Unusual Stage Attire
podcast.body: During their first public performance, Iggy Pop appeared on stage wearing a nightshirt, golf shoes, white mime makeup, and a large afro wig made from tinfoil. "Iggy was wearing a night shirt and golf shoes and white mime makeup and a big afro wig made out of tinfoil."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Iggy's Survival and Drug Dealing (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: During the band's inactive period after being dropped by Elektra, Iggy Pop sustained himself by becoming a middleman for a heroin dealer. However, he often used the drugs himself, exacerbating his addiction. "Iggy paid the bills by becoming a middleman for a hairwind dealer, but sometimes he forgot his role and ended up using all the drugs himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Influence on "Punk" Terminology
podcast.body: Lester Banks, a Detroit rock writer, extensively covered the kind of rock performed by The Stooges and Iggy Pop. His writings helped to shape the early critical understanding of this raw and energetic style of music, which was later associated with the "punk" aesthetic. "Lester Banks began spewing out thousands and thousands of rapturous words on the kind of rock played by the Count Five, Iggy Pop and the Stooges and others of their ilk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

podcast.title: Influence on Kid Rock's Vision
podcast.body: The Stooges were cited by Kid Rock as an influence on his musical vision, which he described as "very white trash Public Enemy style rap, plus The Stooges, plus Kiss, plus Hank Williams." "A vision he calls very white trash public enemy style rap, plus the stooge's plus kiss plus Hank Williams."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 5b: Hip-Hop's Effects Part 2

podcast.title: Influence on Punk Rock
podcast.body: Despite remaining fringe figures, the first three albums by The Stooges, particularly through David Bowie's influence and acceptance of their unconventional style, became fundamental templates for the development of punk rock. Their raw energy and disregard for mainstream rock conventions inspired a new generation of musicians. "And this is how the first three Stooges albums became some of the most important templates for what would be eventually called punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

podcast.title: Influence on Seattle Scene
podcast.body: Tracks from The Stooges were featured on homemade punk cassettes distributed by Buzz Osborne in Aberdeen, Washington, influencing the developing Seattle rock scene. "Buzz Osborne began giving out cassettes featuring his favorite punk songs, All Indie bands, TBI from the stuages, tracks from bad brains and black flag, and Buzz gave these tapes only to people he considered cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: James Williamson's Career Shift
podcast.body: Following the initial breakup, guitarist James Williamson had a brief reunion with Iggy Pop in 1979 but then retired from music to become an electronics engineer. He earned an electrical engineering degree and eventually became the Vice President of Technology Standards for Sony. "He became an electronics engineer, although there was a brief reunion with Iggy in 1979. But then he retired from music, got an electrical engineering degree, and became the vice president of technology standards for Sony."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Most Important Post-Garage Rock Band
podcast.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges were retrospectively identified as the most important of the post-Garage Rock bands. Known for being "drugged out, whacked out, and totally crazy," they were one of the few groups that continued to appeal to audiences after the original Garage Rock sound was thought to be "done" by the late 1960s, and they served as a key inspiration for the first Garage Rock revival (punk). "But in retrospect, the most important of the post garage rock bands, was Iggy Pop and the Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Motor City Ancestor
podcast.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges are cited as "Motor City ancestors" who influenced the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, especially inspiring bands like The White Stripes and Yeah Yeah Yeahs. "From there, they ingratiated themselves into the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, all of whom had something in common with motor city ancestors like the Stooges and the MC5."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Name Change to The Stooges
podcast.body: Shortly after their debut as Iggy and the Psychedelic Stooges, the band's name was shortened to simply "The Stooges," marking the beginning of the legend of Iggy Pop. "The psychedelic studios soon became just the stooages. And here begins the legend of Iggy Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Pioneers of Punk and Alternative Rock
podcast.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges were "absolutely bloody essential" in laying the groundwork for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock music that emerged in subsequent decades, suggesting that the landscape of music would be vastly different without their influence. "Iggy Pop and the Stooges were absolutely bloody essential in setting the stage for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock that was to come in the decades ahead."

podcast.title: Post-Gorilla Incident Demise
podcast.body: Following the bizarre incident with Elton John in the gorilla suit, the mutual admiration between Elton and The Stooges did not lead to a record deal, and the band spiraled towards a breakup, with Iggy Pop deepening his drug use. "Alas, the mutual admiration didn't amount to anything after that. Iggy and the Stooges spiraled towards a breakup, Iggy got deeper into drugs, and Elton never did sign him or the band to a record contract."

podcast.title: Reunion Gap - 29 Years, Two Months, 19 Days
podcast.body: The time between the Stooges' breakup on February 9, 1974, and their reunion at the Coachella Festival on April 27, 2003, totaled 10,670 days, or 29 years, two months, and 19 days, making them the "reunion champions" for the longest hiatus mentioned. "February 9th, 1974 to April 27th, 2003. 10,670 days or 29 years, two months and 19 days from breakup to reunion."

podcast.title: Reunion Overtures and Iggy's Reluctance
podcast.body: For decades after their initial breakup, various attempts were made to reunite Iggy Pop and the Ashton brothers, but Iggy, whose solo career was flourishing and increasingly drug-free, felt revisiting the past would not be in his best interests. "But things were going so well for Iggy that he just felt that it wouldn't be in his best interests to revisit the past."

podcast.body: The Stooges were one of many bands from past decades that reunited in the 21st century, a trend largely motivated by financial incentives. With declining CD sales impacting artist revenues, returning to the touring circuit offered a lucrative way to appeal to nostalgic fan bases and fill large venues. "The list of reunions is long."

podcast.title: Ron Ashton's Estrangement and Side Projects
podcast.body: After the initial breakup of The Stooges, Ron Ashton was estranged from the group due to the "death trip" drug use. "Ron Ashton played in a series of bands, none of which did much, although there was the group that featured Thurston Moore of Sonic Youth, also Mark Arm of Mudhoney and Jay Mascus of Dinosaur Jr."

podcast.title: Ron Ashton's Post-Breakup Career
podcast.body: After the Stooges disbanded, guitarist Ron Ashton played in several bands alongside his brother Scott and also took on minor acting roles in low-budget films. xref.title: Elton John Gorilla Incident (1973)
xref.body: In October 1973, while the Stooges were on a punishing tour and Iggy was heavily incapacitated by Quaaludes, Elton John—dressed in a rented gorilla suit—surprised Iggy on stage at Richard's Club in Atlanta as part of a prank and a potential move to sign the band. Iggy, hallucinating, freaked out believing it was a real gorilla, and the band's guitarist James Williamson almost attacked Elton before his identity was revealed. xref.title: Elton John Gorilla Suit Incident – Richards, Atlanta, October 1973
xref.body: In October 1973, Iggy Pop and the Stooges were playing at Richards in Atlanta at the same time Elton John was touring America. Elton — engaged in a semi-friendly rivalry with David Bowie, who was a known Stooges supporter — decided to crash the show dressed in a full gorilla suit to surprise Iggy on stage. A photographer from Detroit music magazine *Creem* was tipped off. No one warned Iggy that this was planned, and no one warned Elton that Iggy was heavily intoxicated on speed that night. When Elton bounded onto the stage in the gorilla suit, Iggy genuinely believed it was a real gorilla, was terrified, and fled the stage. The incident was captured on film. After Elton removed the gorilla head and multiple people calmed Iggy down, the show resumed and the two performed several songs together — Iggy bare-chested, Elton still in the suit. "Iggy thought it was an actual gorilla. And this freak out is captured on film."

xref.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

xref.body: John Cale of The Velvet Underground was brought in to produce The Stooges' debut record. "He found John Kale, the velvet underground to produce their debut record."

xref.title: Kurt Cobain's Favorite Album
xref.body: Kurt Cobain recorded in his journals that The Stooges' album *Raw Power* was his favorite album ever. "Later, Kurt Cobain recorded in his journals that Raw Power was his favorite album ever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Late 80s/Early 90s Garage Punk Band
xref.body: The Headcoats are cited as an example of a Garage Punk band from the minor revival in the late 1980s and early 1990s. These bands typically played louder and faster, taking more influence from The Stooges than The Kingsmen. "You might have heard of bands like the headcoats and the mighty seasors and the mummies, or maybe not."

xref.title: Late 80s/Early 90s Garage Punk Band
xref.body: The Mighty Caesars are mentioned as a Garage Punk band from the minor revival of the late 1980s and early 1990s, characterized by a louder and faster sound inspired by The Stooges. "You might have heard of bands like the headcoats and the mighty seasors and the mummies, or maybe not."

xref.title: Laying Punk Rock Foundations – Post-Drumming Career
xref.body: Iggy Pop eventually moved from behind the drum kit to start writing songs, leading to the formation of The Stooges. His career further evolved with involvement from David Bowie and significant personal experiences, which collectively laid the foundations for modern punk rock. "He started writing songs moved on to the stooges got involved with David Bowie took a lot of LSD and pretty much laid the foundations for modern punk rock."

xref.title: Longest Hiatus Record (Almost 27 Years)
xref.body: The New York Dolls were apart for almost 27 years, making them one of the bands with the longest gaps between breakup and reunion, surpassed only by The Stooges. "The dolls were a part for almost 27 years, but we can go one further."

xref.title: Meth Injection for Performance
xref.body: During the Elton John gorilla incident, with Iggy Pop incapacitated by Quaaludes, The Stooges' guitarist James Williamson resorted to injecting Iggy with meth to get him on his feet and semi-conscious enough to perform on stage. "He injected Iggy, which was enough to get him on his feet and on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stupid History: The Music Version 1

xref.title: Middleman for Heroin Dealer
xref.body: During The Stooges' inactive period after being dropped by Elektra, Iggy Pop sustained himself financially by acting as a middleman for a heroin dealer. However, he often used the drugs himself, deepening his addiction. "Iggy paid the bills by becoming a middleman for a hairwind dealer, but sometimes he forgot his role and ended up using all the drugs himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Most Important Post-Garage Rock Band
xref.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges were retrospectively identified as the most important of the post-Garage Rock bands. Known for being "drugged out, whacked out, and totally crazy," they were one of the few groups that continued to appeal to audiences after the original Garage Rock sound was thought to be "done" by the late 1960s, and they served as a key inspiration for the first Garage Rock revival (punk). "But in retrospect, the most important of the post garage rock bands, was Iggy Pop and the Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Motor City Ancestor
xref.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges are cited as "Motor City ancestors" who influenced the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, especially inspiring bands like The White Stripes and Yeah Yeah Yeahs. "From there, they ingratiated themselves into the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, all of whom had something in common with motor city ancestors like the Stooges and the MC5."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Musical Vision
xref.body: Kid Rock had a distinct musical vision, which he described as "very white trash Public Enemy style rap, plus The Stooges, plus Kiss, plus Hank Williams," reflecting his broad influences and status as a "big country fan." "He had this vision. A vision he calls very white trash public enemy style rap, plus the stooge's plus kiss plus Hank Williams. Like I said, he's a big country fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 5b: Hip-Hop's Effects Part 2

xref.title: Nihilistic Parallel with The Stooges
xref.body: The Velvet Underground are noted for being as nihilistic as Iggy Pop and The Stooges, establishing a parallel in their challenging and dark artistic approach. "They were every bit as nihilistic as the Velvet Underground and violent to boot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Outrageous Behavior
xref.body: Iggy Pop was known for his "outrageous behavior" and "extreme things" performed with his band The Stooges in America, which directly influenced David Bowie's creation of the Ziggy Stardust character. "Iggy Pop, who was doing all kinds of extreme things in America with his band, The Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Patronage of Iggy Pop and The Stooges
xref.body: Bowie was a great admirer and musical hero of Iggy Pop, fascinated by his craziness, almost constant mental instability, and ability to see beyond the drugs and self-destructive stage antics to Iggy's intelligence. Bowie convinced his manager to take on Iggy and The Stooges as a project, providing a cash injection that funded their *Raw Power* album. He later visited Iggy when he was in a mental hospital. Bowie's acceptance of Iggy also helped propel the first three Stooges albums to become important templates for punk rock. "Iggy's craziness had made him into one of Bowie's musical heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

xref.title: Played Bass on *The Weirdness*
xref.body: Punk stalwart Mike Watt joined The Stooges to play bass on their reunion album, *The Weirdness*, released in 2007. "On base was punk stalwart Mike Watt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Post-Performance Stage Condition
xref.body: After The Stooges' performances, the stage was typically "slick with blood" due to Iggy Pop's self-mutilation and violent antics. This visual aftermath underscored the raw and dangerous nature of their live shows. "And no wonder when the stooages left the stage, it was slick with blood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Post-Prime Movers Blues Focus
xref.body: After leaving The Prime Movers, Iggy initially focused on becoming a better blues player before reuniting with the Ashton brothers and Dave Alexander, which led to the formation of The Stooges. "He left the prime movers shortly after that to concentrate on being a better blues player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Post-Stooges Mental Health Crisis
xref.body: After The Stooges disbanded, Iggy Pop's mental and physical state deteriorated, leading him to a psychiatric hospital in Los Angeles. He was described as a "babbling, strung out freak prone to blockouts and random acts of violence," eventually disappearing and being found in a "heap under the counter at a hamburger joint," where police gave him the choice of jail or a long stint in a mental unit. "When the Stooages finally blew apart, Iggy had nowhere to go but a psychiatric hospital in Los Angeles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Post-Stooges Success and Nickname
xref.body: After the Stooges' breakup, Iggy Pop eventually cleaned up, launched a successful solo career, earned millions by licensing his music like "Lust for Life," and acquired the legendary title of "The Godfather of Punk." "The big surprise was Iggy. He cleaned up eventually. He started a solar career and has made millions upon millions of dollars licensing lust for life and use and cruise ship commercials. He also managed to acquire the legendary title of The Godfather of Punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

xref.title: Rivalry with David Bowie
xref.body: In the early 1970s, Elton John was in a friendly competition with his friend David Bowie over who could be the biggest British rock star. Bowie was also friends with Iggy Pop and working with The Stooges, influencing Elton's desire to prank Bowie and potentially sign The Stooges. "At the time, Elton was in competition with his friend David Bowie over who could be the biggest British rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stupid History: The Music Version 1

xref.title: Savior of The Stooges
xref.body: Leveraging his influence and industry power, David Bowie convinced Iggy Pop and the Ashton brothers, along with James Williamson, to move to England to record the *Raw Power* album for Columbia Records, effectively restarting The Stooges' career. "Bowie, although not in the greatest shape himself when it came to drugs, turned out to be Iggy's and ultimately the studio's savior."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Soviet Blacklist - Violence
xref.body: This band was listed on the USSR's 1985 "not recommended music" list due to associations with "Violence," with the possibility that the Soviet authorities mistakenly referred to Iggy Pop and The Stooges. Their inclusion reflects the Soviet Union's concerns about the perceived aggressive or disruptive nature of certain Western rock acts. "The Stages, I think they meant Iggy Pop and the Stooges, Violence, ACDC, Neo-Fascism and Violence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Conspiracy

xref.title: Soviet Blacklist Entry – Violence
xref.body: Referred to as "The Stages," presumably meaning Iggy Pop and The Stooges, this band was listed on the Soviet Union's 1985 "not recommended music" list due to themes of "violence." "The Stages, I think they meant Iggy Pop and the Stooges, Violence."

srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

xref.title: Struggling for Image and Sound (Late 1960s)
xref.body: Around the time The Velvet Underground, The Stooges, MC5, and Captain Beefheart were making records, David Bowie was struggling to define his own image, style, and sound, without much success. "Well, he was trying to find himself. He was trying to come up with an image and a style and a sound that would work for him and he wasn't doing very well."

xref.title: Unconventional Drumming
xref.body: As the drummer for The Stooges, Scott Asheton employed an unconventional drumming style, keeping time by banging on 50-gallon oil drums using hammers instead of standard drumsticks. "Drummer Scott Ashden kept time by banging on a couple of 50 gallon oil drums with hammers instead of drumsticks."
